title: Data Science Foundations
description: What data science actually involves day to day, how tabular data is organized, and your first steps with pandas.

lessons.title: What Data Scientists Actually Do
lessons.description: Get a clear picture of the data science workflow, from question to decision.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe the typical data science workflow and where most of the real work actually happens.

sections.title: 🔍 It starts with a question, not a dataset
sections.content:
Good data science starts with a business or research question: "why are customers cancelling?", "which patients are at risk?", "will this ad campaign work?" The data comes second — you collect or find data that can actually answer the question.

Jumping straight to "let's build a model" without a clear question is one of the most common ways projects go nowhere.

sections.title: 🔄 The typical workflow
sections.content:
Most data science work follows a loop, not a straight line:

• **Ask** a specific, answerable question
• **Collect** the relevant data
• **Clean** it — this is almost always the biggest chunk of the work
• **Explore** it to find patterns and sanity-check assumptions
• **Model** it, if a model is actually needed
• **Communicate** the result clearly so someone can act on it

You often loop back — exploring the data reveals a cleaning problem, or modeling reveals you need different data.

sections.title: 🧹 The unglamorous truth: it's mostly cleaning
sections.content:
Surveys of data scientists consistently find that **60-80% of project time** goes into collecting, cleaning, and reshaping data — not building fancy models. That's normal, not a sign you're doing something wrong.

```python
import pandas as pd

# A tiny taste of what's coming — reading a table of data
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer": ["Ana", "Bo", "Chen"],
    "purchases": [5, None, 12],
})
print(df)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Skipping straight to modeling.** A fancy model trained on messy, misunderstood data gives confidently wrong answers.

**Not defining the question clearly.** "Analyze the data" isn't a question — "which factors predict churn in the first 30 days" is.

**Treating one pass through the workflow as final.** Real projects loop back through cleaning and exploring multiple times as you learn more.

questions.question: What typically takes up the largest share of a data science project's time?
options: Building the model
Collecting, cleaning, and reshaping data
Presenting results
Choosing a programming language
questions.explanation: Cleaning and preparing data is consistently reported as the most time-consuming part of real-world data science work — often 60-80% of total effort.

questions.question: Why should a data science project start with a question rather than a dataset?
options: Questions are required by law
A clear question guides what data to collect and how to judge success
Datasets are always messy
It's faster to start with data
questions.explanation: Starting from a specific question keeps the project focused — it tells you what data actually matters and what a useful answer would look like.

questions.question: Which best describes the data science workflow?
options: A strict one-way pipeline that never repeats
A loop where cleaning and exploring often send you back to earlier steps
Modeling first, then collecting data
Skipping straight from question to communication
questions.explanation: In practice, work loops back constantly — exploring data might reveal a cleaning issue, or modeling might reveal you need different data entirely.

questions.question: What does the 'communicate' step at the end of the workflow actually involve?
options: Rebuilding the model from scratch
Presenting the results clearly so someone can understand and act on them
Deleting the raw data files
Writing unit tests for the code
questions.explanation: Communication turns analysis into something decision-makers can actually use — a clear takeaway they can act on, not just a pile of numbers.

questions.question: Is building a model always a required step in data science work?
options: Yes, every project must end with a trained model
No — sometimes a clear answer comes from exploration and simple statistics without needing a model at all
Only if the dataset has more than 1000 rows
Only when working with numeric data
questions.explanation: Not every question needs a model — sometimes careful exploration and summary statistics are enough to answer the business question directly.

questions.question: What's a realistic example of the workflow 'looping back'?
options: Finishing communication and never touching the project again
Discovering during exploration that a column has inconsistent values, so you go back to cleaning before continuing
Always redoing the entire project from scratch each time
Skipping the question step entirely
questions.explanation: It's common to discover a data quality issue while exploring, which sends you back to the cleaning step before you can trust further analysis.

questions.question: Why does jumping straight to 'let's build a model' often cause projects to stall?
options: Models always take too long to train
Without a clear question, there's no way to define what a good model result would even mean
Models can only be built after cleaning is finished
It's technically impossible to build a model without a question
questions.explanation: Without a well-defined question, there's no clear target or success criterion to build toward, so the modeling effort has nothing concrete to aim at.

questions.question: Which is an example of a well-defined data science question?
options: "Analyze the data"
"Which factors predict customer churn in the first 30 days?"
"Make a dashboard"
"Look at the numbers"
questions.explanation: A well-defined question names a specific outcome (churn), a specific scope (first 30 days), and something answerable from data (factors that predict it).

lessons.title: Rows, Columns, and Data Types
lessons.description: Learn how tabular data is organized and why data types matter before you analyze anything.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe a tabular dataset's structure and identify common data types found in each column.

sections.title: 📋 Tabular data: rows and columns
sections.content:
Most real-world data science works with **tabular data** — think of a spreadsheet. Each **row** is one observation (a customer, a transaction, a sensor reading). Each **column** is one attribute of that observation (age, price, timestamp).

• Rows are often called *records* or *observations*
• Columns are often called *fields*, *features*, or *variables*
• A well-organized table has one consistent meaning per column

sections.title: 🔢 Common data types
sections.content:
Every column has a **data type** that determines what you can do with it:

• **Numeric** — ages, prices, counts (can compute averages, sums)
• **Categorical** — country, product type, status (a fixed set of labels)
• **Boolean** — true/false flags
• **Datetime** — timestamps, dates
• **Text** — free-form strings like reviews or comments

Getting the data type wrong causes real bugs — treating a ZIP code as a number lets you "average" ZIP codes, which is meaningless.

sections.title: 🗂️ Why structure matters before analysis
sections.content:
Before analyzing anything, it helps to ask: what does one row represent? Is it one customer, or one order (a customer might have many)? Mixing up the row's meaning is a common source of subtly wrong analysis.

```python
import pandas as pd

data = {
    "order_id": [1, 2, 3],
    "customer": ["Ana", "Ana", "Bo"],
    "amount": [50.0, 20.0, 75.0],
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df.dtypes)
# order_id      int64
# customer     object
# amount      float64
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Not checking data types before analyzing.** A column that looks numeric might actually be stored as text (e.g. "1,200" with a comma), silently breaking calculations.

**Confusing what a row represents.** "One row per order" and "one row per customer" need very different aggregation logic.

**Treating categorical codes as numbers.** A "status" column coded 1/2/3 shouldn't be averaged — the numbers are just labels.

questions.question: In a table of customer orders where each row is one order, what does a single row represent?
options: One customer
One product in the catalog
One order (a customer can have many rows)
One day of business
questions.explanation: If each row is an order, a single customer could appear in multiple rows — once per order they placed.

questions.question: Why is it a problem to store a ZIP code as a numeric data type?
options: ZIP codes don't exist as numbers
Averaging or summing ZIP codes produces meaningless results since they're really labels, not quantities
Numeric types use more memory
It's not actually a problem
questions.explanation: ZIP codes are identifiers, not quantities — operations like averaging them don't make sense even though they're written with digits.

questions.question: What's a good first question to ask before analyzing a new tabular dataset?
options: What color should the chart be?
What does a single row actually represent?
How many charts will I need?
What's the file format?
questions.explanation: Understanding what one row means (one customer? one order? one event?) shapes every aggregation and analysis decision that follows.

questions.question: In a tabular dataset, what does a column typically represent?
options: A single record or observation
An attribute or measurement shared across all rows, like 'price' or 'city'
The total number of rows
A single cell's value
questions.explanation: Each column typically holds one particular attribute measured or recorded for every row, like age, price, or city.

questions.question: What are the four broad categories of data types commonly found in tabular data?
options: Rows, columns, cells, and tables
Numeric, categorical, datetime, and text
Positive, negative, zero, and undefined
CSV, JSON, Excel, and SQL
questions.explanation: Tabular datasets typically mix numeric (quantities), categorical (labels), datetime (timestamps), and text (free-form strings) data types.

questions.question: Why does understanding a dataset's 'grain' (what one row represents) matter before joining it to another table?
options: It doesn't matter — joins work regardless of grain
Joining tables with mismatched grains can silently duplicate or miscount rows
Grain only matters for numeric columns
It's only relevant when using SQL, not pandas
questions.explanation: If one table is at the order level and another is at the customer level, joining them naively can multiply rows unexpectedly, corrupting downstream counts and sums.

questions.question: What's an example of a row-grain mistake leading to double counting?
options: Averaging a column that has no missing values
Joining an orders table to a products table without first aggregating, then summing revenue and getting inflated totals
Selecting a single column from a DataFrame
Renaming a column
questions.explanation: If a join produces multiple rows per original order (say, one row per line item) and you then sum the order-level total column, you'll overcount because that total repeats across the new rows.

questions.question: What's the difference between continuous and categorical numeric data?
options: They are the same thing
Continuous numeric data can take any value in a range (like price); categorical numeric data represents discrete labels even though it's stored as numbers (like a zip code or ID)
Categorical numeric data can only be negative
Continuous data must always be integers
questions.explanation: Some numeric-looking columns, like zip codes or customer IDs, are really categorical labels rather than quantities you'd average or sum — the type looks numeric but the meaning isn't.

lessons.title: Meet Pandas: Series and DataFrames
lessons.description: Get comfortable with the two core building blocks of Python's most popular data tool.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can create a pandas Series and DataFrame and explain the difference between them.

sections.title: 🐼 Why pandas?
sections.content: **Pandas** is the standard Python library for working with tabular data. It gives you fast, convenient tools for loading, filtering, transforming, and summarizing data — instead of writing loops over lists of lists by hand.

sections.title: 📏 Series: a single labeled column
sections.content:
A **Series** is a one-dimensional array with labels (an *index*) attached to each value — like a single labeled column.

```python
import pandas as pd

ages = pd.Series([25, 31, 42], index=["Ana", "Bo", "Chen"])
print(ages["Bo"])   # 31
print(ages.mean())  # 32.666...
```

sections.title: 📊 DataFrame: a full table
sections.content:
A **DataFrame** is a two-dimensional table — a collection of Series sharing the same index, basically a spreadsheet. It's the structure you'll use for almost everything.

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Ana", "Bo", "Chen"],
    "age": [25, 31, 42],
    "city": ["Lahore", "Karachi", "Lahore"],
})
print(df)
print(df["age"])       # selects one column as a Series
print(df.shape)        # (3, 3) — 3 rows, 3 columns
```

• Each column of a DataFrame is a Series
• `df["col"]` selects a single column
• `df.shape` tells you (rows, columns)

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Confusing a Series with a plain list.** A Series carries an index, which is what makes lookups by label and alignment between columns work.

**Forgetting `df.shape` and `df.columns` when starting out.** These two quick checks catch a surprising number of "why is my data wrong" bugs early.

**Modifying a DataFrame and being surprised the original didn't change.** Many pandas operations return a *new* DataFrame by default instead of changing it in place.

questions.question: What is a pandas Series?
options: A two-dimensional table
A one-dimensional labeled array — like a single column
A type of chart
A CSV file
questions.explanation: A Series is one-dimensional with an index attached to each value — think of it as a single labeled column of data.

questions.question: What does `df.shape` return for a DataFrame with 100 rows and 5 columns?
questions.explanation: `.shape` returns a tuple of (number of rows, number of columns) — here, (100, 5).

questions.question: What is a DataFrame best described as?
options: A single number
A two-dimensional table made of columns that are each a Series
A type of loop
A database connection
questions.explanation: A DataFrame is pandas' core table structure — a collection of aligned Series (columns) sharing the same row index.

questions.question: How do you access a single column of a DataFrame as a Series?
options: df.column('name')
df['column_name']
df.get_row('column_name')
df.column_name.values()
questions.explanation: Using square-bracket indexing with the column name, like df['column_name'], returns that column as a Series.

questions.question: How does a DataFrame relate to a Series?
options: They are unrelated data structures
A DataFrame can be thought of as a collection of Series objects sharing the same index, one per column
A Series is a special kind of DataFrame with two dimensions
A DataFrame can only ever hold one Series
questions.explanation: Each column of a DataFrame is itself a Series, and the DataFrame combines many of them side-by-side, all sharing the same row index.

questions.question: What do `df.columns` and `df.index` return?
options: The actual data values in the DataFrame
The labels for the DataFrame's columns and rows, respectively
The number of rows and columns
A copy of the entire DataFrame
questions.explanation: `df.columns` gives the column labels and `df.index` gives the row labels, letting you inspect the DataFrame's structure without looking at the data itself.

questions.question: Why is pandas generally preferred over plain Python lists and dictionaries for tabular data?
options: Pandas is required by Python itself
Pandas provides fast, vectorized operations and built-in tools for filtering, grouping, and cleaning tabular data
Lists and dictionaries can't store numbers
Pandas uses less memory than any other approach in every case
questions.explanation: Pandas offers purpose-built, efficient operations for tabular data — filtering, aggregating, merging — that would require much more manual code with plain lists and dicts.

questions.question: What's the difference between `df['col']` and `df[['col']]`?
options: There is no difference between them
`df['col']` returns a Series, while `df[['col']]` returns a DataFrame with just that one column
`df[['col']]` is invalid syntax
`df['col']` always raises an error
questions.explanation: Single brackets with one column name return a Series, while double brackets (a list of column names) return a DataFrame, even with just one column selected.

lessons.title: Loading and First-Look Inspection
lessons.description: Learn the handful of commands you run on every new dataset before doing anything else.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can load a CSV file and run a quick first-look inspection to understand its shape and quality.

sections.title: 📂 Loading data
sections.content:
The most common way to bring data into pandas is `read_csv`, which reads a comma-separated file straight into a DataFrame.

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
```

Pandas can also read Excel files, JSON, and databases — but CSV is the format you'll see constantly.

sections.title: 👀 The first-look checklist
sections.content:
Before doing anything else with a new dataset, run this quick checklist:

```python
print(df.shape)     # how many rows and columns?
print(df.head())    # what do the first few rows look like?
print(df.info())    # data types and how many non-null values per column
print(df.describe())  # count, mean, std, min, max for numeric columns
```

• `.head()` catches obviously wrong data early (wrong file, wrong delimiter)
• `.info()` shows data types and flags columns with missing values
• `.describe()` gives a fast sanity check — does the min/max make sense?

sections.title: 🚩 Spotting red flags early
sections.content:
This first look often reveals problems before you've written a single line of analysis:

• A numeric column showing up as `object` (text) type — probably has stray characters like commas or currency symbols
• `.describe()` showing a minimum age of -5 or a maximum of 200 — clearly bad data
• `.info()` showing far fewer non-null values than total rows — missing data to handle

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Skipping the first look and jumping straight into analysis.** Five minutes of `.head()`, `.info()`, and `.describe()` regularly saves hours of debugging wrong conclusions.

**Ignoring `.describe()`'s min/max values.** Impossible values (negative ages, 999999 placeholders) are often hiding right there.

**Assuming the file loaded correctly without checking `.shape`.** A wrong delimiter can silently load everything into a single column.

questions.question: Which pandas function reads a comma-separated file into a DataFrame?
options: pd.read_csv()
pd.load_table()
pd.import_data()
pd.open_csv()
questions.explanation: `pd.read_csv()` is the standard way to load a CSV file into a pandas DataFrame.

questions.question: What does `.describe()` help you catch early?
options: Spelling mistakes in column names
Impossible values like negative ages or absurd maximums
The file's creation date
The number of columns only
questions.explanation: `.describe()` shows min/max/mean for numeric columns, which is a fast way to spot data that's clearly wrong, like negative ages.

questions.question: A column of prices shows up as `object` (text) type instead of numeric. What's the most likely cause?
options: The prices are too large for a number
The column probably contains stray characters like $ signs or commas
Pandas doesn't support prices
The file is corrupted beyond use
questions.explanation: Currency symbols, commas, or other non-numeric characters in a column force pandas to treat it as text rather than a number — a very common first-look catch.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `.head()` and `.tail()`?
options: To delete the first or last rows
To quickly preview the first or last few rows of a DataFrame
To count the total number of rows
To sort the DataFrame
questions.explanation: `.head()` and `.tail()` give a fast visual preview of a few rows from the start or end of the data, useful for a first sanity check.

questions.question: What does `.info()` show about a DataFrame?
options: Only the column names
Column names, non-null counts, and data types for every column, in one summary
Just the number of rows
Only the file path the data was loaded from
questions.explanation: `.info()` gives a compact overview of every column's data type and how many non-missing values it has, which is a fast way to spot problems.

questions.question: Why is checking data types right after loading a dataset a good habit?
options: It's not important — types can be ignored
A column that should be numeric might have loaded as text, which silently breaks any math or sorting done on it later
Data types never change after loading
It only matters for very large files
questions.explanation: Catching a type mismatch early — like a price column loaded as text — avoids subtle bugs and wrong results further down the analysis.

questions.question: Why is checking `df.shape` a useful first-look step?
options: It shows the actual data values
It quickly confirms how many rows and columns loaded, which can catch a botched or partial load
It sorts the data automatically
It only works after cleaning
questions.explanation: Comparing the loaded shape against what you expected (e.g. a known row count) is a fast sanity check that the file loaded completely and correctly.

questions.question: Why should checking for missing values be part of the first-look checklist rather than something you do much later?
options: Missing values can't be checked until modeling
Discovering missing data early shapes decisions about cleaning, and surprises later can undermine trust in results already produced
Missing values are always automatically filled by pandas
It's not actually useful to check early
questions.explanation: Knowing early how much data is missing, and where, lets you plan cleaning decisions upfront instead of discovering a serious gap after analysis is already underway.
